title.source: Why did independence follow different paths?

essentialQuestion.source: How can dated records help us compare two paths to independence without ranking them?

learningGoal.source: Compare dated records of how Indonesia and the Federation of Malaya became independent, and explain why a proclamation and a transfer of sovereignty are different events.

warmUp.question.source: Can a country have more than one big date in its story of becoming free?

evidence.question.source: What does each source record? Who made it, and when?

evidence.cards.0.sources.0.caption.source: Source 1: Sukarno's handwritten draft of the proclamation of independence, 17 August 1945

evidence.cards.0.sources.0.details.0.source: A short text, written by hand by Sukarno, declaring Indonesia's independence.

evidence.cards.0.sources.0.details.1.source: It is kept by Indonesia's National Archives (ANRI). In 2020 the President's office borrowed it for the 17 August ceremony at the palace, then returned it.

evidence.cards.0.sources.0.details.2.source: Limit: it records the 1945 declaration. It does not tell us about the talks, the fighting or people's lives from 1945 to 1949.

evidence.cards.0.sources.1.caption.source: Source 2: Records of the transfer of sovereignty, 27 December 1949 (described by the National Archives of the Netherlands)

evidence.cards.0.sources.1.details.0.source: A conference in The Hague met from 23 August to 2 November 1949.

evidence.cards.0.sources.1.details.1.source: The Netherlands transferred sovereignty on 27 December 1949.

evidence.cards.0.sources.1.details.2.source: Limit: these records come from the government that had ruled the colony. They show a formal step, not how Indonesians saw it.

evidence.cards.0.sources.2.caption.source: Source 3: The London Agreement, signed on 8 February 1956 (described by the Government of Malaysia)

evidence.cards.0.sources.2.details.0.source: Signed by leaders of the Federation of Malaya and Britain.

evidence.cards.0.sources.2.details.1.source: It set 31 August 1957 as the day the Federation of Malaya would become independent.

evidence.cards.0.sources.2.details.2.source: Limit: it records what leaders agreed, not what every person thought.

evidence.cards.0.sources.3.caption.source: Source 4: A newsreel film of the independence ceremony in Kuala Lumpur, 1957, made by British Pathé

evidence.cards.0.sources.3.details.0.source: Made by a British film company on the day of the ceremony at Stadium Merdeka.

evidence.cards.0.sources.3.details.1.source: Its shot list describes crowds, guests arriving, speeches and the Federation's flag being raised.

evidence.cards.0.sources.3.details.2.source: Limit: the camera chose what to show. It shows the ceremony, not the years of talks before it.

evidence.cards.0.sources.4.caption.source: Source 5: A photo of Stadium Merdeka, Kuala Lumpur, taken on 9 February 2025 by Renek78

evidence.cards.0.sources.4.details.0.source: It shows people watching a football match inside the stadium.

evidence.cards.0.sources.4.details.1.source: Limit: it shows the place in 2025, not the 1957 ceremony.

read.sections.0.text.source: On 17 August 1945, two leaders, Sukarno and Mohammad Hatta, made a proclamation of independence for Indonesia. The country's National Archives keeps Sukarno's handwritten draft of this short text. For Indonesians, 17 August 1945 is the day of independence. But the Netherlands had ruled the islands as a colony, and it did not accept the proclamation. Years of armed struggle and talks followed. On 27 December 1949, the Netherlands transferred sovereignty. This was a different event from the proclamation. It came after a long struggle. The draft records the 1945 statement. It does not tell us about every talk, or how people lived through those years.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: On 17 August 1945, two leaders made a proclamation. They said Indonesia was free. The two men were Sukarno and Hatta. Sukarno wrote the first draft by hand. The national archives keep it today. The Dutch had ruled the islands as a colony. They did not accept the proclamation. Years of fighting and talks came next. In December 1949, the Dutch passed sovereignty to the new state. That was a new step, not the first one. But for the people there, 1945 is still the year they became free.

read.sections.1.text.source: The Federation of Malaya took a different path. On 8 February 1956, its leaders and Britain signed an agreement in London. It set 31 August 1957 as the day of independence. These are not two rival dates. One is the date of an agreement, and one is the date it planned for. The new country was the Federation of Malaya. Malaysia, a larger federation, was formed later, on 16 September 1963. A path built on talks still had conflict. A long armed conflict called the Malayan Emergency began in 1948. It was declared over only in 1960.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: Malaya took a different path. In 1956, its leaders and Britain signed an agreement in London. It set a date. On 31 August 1957, the Federation of Malaya became free. A federation is a group of states that work as one. Malaysia came later, in 1963. Malaya's path used talks. But there was also a long armed conflict. It began in 1948. It did not end until 1960.

read.sections.2.heading.source: Compare evidence, not countries as winners

read.sections.2.text.source: The two paths had different people, papers, conflicts and choices. A proclamation, an agreement and a ceremony each record a different part of change. The photo shows Stadium Merdeka in Kuala Lumpur in 2025. It shows the place, not the 1957 ceremony. A British news film made on the day shows crowds, guests and the Federation's flag going up. When you compare sources, ask three questions. What happened on this date? Who made the source? What came later? A careful look can show how two paths differ, without calling one of them better.

read.sections.2.simpler.source: The two paths had different people and choices. A proclamation, an agreement and a ceremony each show one part of the story. The photo shows a stadium in 2025. It does not show the 1957 ceremony. A British film from 1957 shows crowds and a new flag going up. Ask three questions about each source. What happened on this date? Who made it? What came after? Do not say one path was better.

read.glossary.0.definition.source: A public statement that tells everyone about something important.

read.glossary.0.example.source: Sukarno and Hatta made a proclamation of independence in 1945.

read.glossary.1.definition.source: The power of a state to rule itself.

read.glossary.1.example.source: In December 1949, the Netherlands transferred sovereignty to Indonesia.

read.glossary.2.definition.source: A place ruled by a country far away.

read.glossary.2.example.source: The Netherlands had ruled the islands of Indonesia as a colony.

read.glossary.3.definition.source: A decision that two or more groups make together and sign.

read.glossary.3.example.source: An agreement signed in London in 1956 set Malaya's independence day.

read.glossary.4.definition.source: A group of states joined under one main government.

read.glossary.4.example.source: The Federation of Malaya became independent in 1957.

write.prompt.source: Name one dated record for each country. Then say why a proclamation and a transfer of sovereignty are not the same.

write.sentenceStarters.1.source: For the Federation of Malaya, one dated record is ...

write.selfCheck.0.source: I named one dated record for each country.

write.selfCheck.1.source: I explained why the two events are different.

write.selfCheck.2.source: I did not call one path better.

write.example.source: For Indonesia, one dated record is the proclamation of 17 August 1945. The national archives keep Sukarno's draft of it. For Malaya, one dated record is the agreement signed in London in 1956. It set 31 August 1957 as the day Malaya became free. A proclamation is a public statement by the country's own leaders. A transfer of sovereignty is a later step. It is when the old ruler hands over power. Neither source tells us how every person lived in these years.

speak.partnerTask.source: With a partner, explain why the two timelines have different dates. Do not rank them: say what each date records.

speak.independentTask.source: Make a short spoken or written outline: two dates for Indonesia, two for Malaya, and what each one records.

watch.why.source: This short newsreel was filmed at the 1957 ceremony in Stadium Merdeka, so you can compare a source made on the day with the 2025 photo of the same place.

watch.beforeQuestion.source: What would you expect to see at an independence ceremony?

watch.afterQuestion.source: What is raised near the end of the film, and what do the guests do?

watch.summary.source: This short film was made in 1957 in Kuala Lumpur by British Pathé, a British company that made news films. It shows the ceremony for the independence of the Federation of Malaya. First, the camera looks down on Stadium Merdeka. The stadium is full of people, and many of them hold umbrellas. Cars arrive, and important guests walk in. The camera moves between the guests and the crowds. People make speeches from a raised stage. Guards stand very still around the field. Near the end, the flag of the Federation is raised. The important guests salute it as it reaches the top of the pole. The film shows one day. It does not show the years of talks that came before it.

watch.keyPoints.0.source: The film was made in Kuala Lumpur in 1957 by British Pathé, a British news film company.

watch.keyPoints.1.source: It shows crowds at Stadium Merdeka, guests arriving and speeches.

watch.keyPoints.2.source: Near the end, the Federation's flag is raised and the guests salute it.

watch.contentNote.source: Not yet watched by a person. Title and channel confirmed with YouTube's oEmbed on 1 November 2026; length (2:16) from YouTube's listing. The summary is based only on British Pathé's shot list in the video's description (film ID 2888.24), not on the film or its captions: check whether it has sound or narration and what any narration says. It shows only the Malaya part of the lesson. It is a British company's record of the day, so ask who made it and what it might leave out. The shot list names one group in the crowd by ethnicity; the summary does not. Check for advertising before the video.

visual.alt.source: Two timelines side by side. Indonesia: proclamation on 17 August 1945, then struggle and talks, then transfer of sovereignty on 27 December 1949. Federation of Malaya: agreement signed on 8 February 1956, independence on 31 August 1957, Malaysia formed on 16 September 1963, with the Malayan Emergency shown from 1948 to 1960.

sensitiveNotes.0.source: Both paths involved armed conflict: Indonesia's struggle of 1945–1949 and the Malayan Emergency of 1948–1960. The lesson names this plainly and gives no detail; keep it that way, and show no images of fighting. Many popular YouTube videos on Indonesia's revolution show combat and dead bodies, so do not swap one in for the Watch video. Never ask learners about their own or their family's experiences of war, conflict or displacement, or about their home country, religion or ethnicity, and never ask them to compare their own country's history with these. Learners and staff in Indonesia or Malaysia may feel strongly about these dates: present each as that country's own history, not a contest.

educatorNotes.0.source: Aim: learners compare dated records for the two paths without ranking them. Evidence move: separate 1945 and 1949 for Indonesia, and 1956 and 1957 for the Federation of Malaya, then name 1963 for Malaysia. A sound answer gives a dated comparison and never says that one nation's independence depended only on outside recognition. Misconceptions to address: "Indonesia was only independent in 1949", "Malaya's path had no conflict", and calling 1957 "Malaysia's independence".

educatorNotes.1.source: Source caveats: Indonesians count independence from 17 August 1945. For decades the Netherlands named 27 December 1949 instead; the Dutch National Archives' teaching page notes that in 2023 the Dutch prime minister said the Netherlands fully accepts that Indonesia became independent on 17 August 1945. The 1949 transfer was to the federal Republic of the United States of Indonesia, replaced by the unitary Republic a year later: keep this in your notes, not as another date for learners. Malaysia was formed in 1963 by the Federation of Malaya, Singapore, Sabah and Sarawak (Brunei did not join). Government and archive pages on both sides use celebratory language; treat it as their perspective. FINAS's long film "Merdeka for Malaya" (1958) is a state-produced source to analyse, not a Watch video, and do not reproduce the National Archives of Malaysia's 1957 photograph without its reuse permission.
